title: New US Bill Would Strip H-1B Visa of Green Card Pathway
excerpt: The American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act, introduced by Republican Congressman Chip Roy, proposes to eliminate the H-1B visa's dual-intent provision and shorten its maximum duration to two years, threatening the immigration plans of hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals.
body:
• The American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act would eliminate the H-1B visa's ability to serve as a pathway to permanent residency in the US
  • The bill would shorten the maximum H-1B duration from six years to two years and replace the lottery system with a salary-based selection
  • It would also scrap the Optional Practical Training program that allows international students to work in the US after graduation
  • The legislation comes as Indian nationals face an estimated 89-year wait for employment-based green cards under current per-country caps

A Direct Challenge to Dual Intent

A new bill introduced in the United States House of Representatives aims to fundamentally reshape the H-1B visa program by eliminating its most valued feature: the ability to serve as a stepping stone to permanent residency. The American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act, introduced on June 4 by Republican Congressman Chip Roy of Texas, proposes sweeping changes that would affect hundreds of thousands of Indian technology professionals.

The bill targets what is known as the "dual intent" provision, a longstanding policy under which H-1B visa holders can work temporarily in the United States while simultaneously pursuing a green card. Under the proposed legislation, H-1B applicants would be required to demonstrate that they maintain a residence abroad and do not intend to abandon it — effectively treating the work visa as purely temporary.

"For its nearly forty-year history, the H-1B visa has been abused, allowing employers to routinely sideline American STEM workers in favour of cheap foreign labour, while masking layoffs and wage suppression as 'shortages.'"

— Congressman Chip Roy (R-Texas)

Shorter Stays, Higher Bars

Beyond ending the green card pathway, the bill proposes to cut the maximum H-1B visa duration from six years to two years, a change that would drastically limit the time foreign workers can remain in the United States on a single visa cycle. It would also replace the current lottery-based selection system with one that prioritizes applicants whose employers offer higher salaries, a shift designed to counter what critics describe as wage suppression through cheaper foreign labor.

The legislation would additionally repeal provisions that allow H-1B holders to extend their status while awaiting green card processing — a mechanism currently used by hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals stuck in the employment-based green card backlog. It would also scrap the Optional Practical Training program, which allows international students to work in the United States for up to three years after graduation in STEM fields.

The bill has drawn support from organizations including the Immigration Accountability Project, the Federation for American Immigration Reform, and US Tech Workers. "The bill will effectively address many of the egregious aspects of the H-1B visa programme that have not merely encouraged but enabled corporations, universities, and NGOs to displace our most productive workers," said Kevin Lynn, president of US Tech Workers.

The Backlog That Won't Move

The proposed legislation arrives at a particularly fraught moment for Indian professionals navigating the US immigration system. Indian nationals currently face the longest employment-based green card backlog of any nationality, with approximately 800,000 pending petitions and an estimated wait time of 89 years in the EB-2 and EB-3 categories, according to analysis by the Bipartisan Policy Center.

The per-country cap system, which limits any single nation to 7% of the 140,000 employment-based green cards available annually, means Indian nationals can receive only about 9,800 green cards per year despite generating a disproportionate share of applications. Dependent spouses and children are also affected, with children at risk of "aging out" of their dependent status when they turn 21.

Separately, the EAGLE Act — a bipartisan bill that would phase out per-country caps over nine years — passed the House earlier this year and is being considered in the Senate. The two pieces of legislation represent opposing visions for the future of employment-based immigration, with Indian professionals caught between proposals that would either dramatically improve or severely restrict their path to permanent residency.

Roy, who represents Texas's 21st Congressional District, is retiring from Congress. Arizona Republican Congressman Eli Crane, a co-sponsor, said the bill "delivers significant reforms that protect future generations instead of padding bottom lines at their expense."
